title: Nayanthara, Kiara, Tara, Huma, Rukmini: Five Queens Just Entered the World of Toxic
excerpt: Yash's most anticipated post-KGF film finally reveals its leading ladies — and the 'Ladies & Ladies' teaser makes it clear this fairy tale isn't for children
body:
Key Takeaways
  • The teaser for *Toxic* reveals five strong female leads, each with distinct characters.
  • Yash returns after a four-year absence, playing a dual role in this pan-India film.
  • The film is shot in Kannada and English, with dubbed versions in multiple languages.
  • Audience reactions are polarized, with excitement and skepticism about the film's aesthetic.
  • The release on August 26 aims to connect with NRI audiences through a multi-lingual strategy.
Meet the Queens of Toxic
›Nayanthara as Ganga: Commanding authority.
›Kiara Advani as Nadia: Vulnerable yet intense.
›Tara Sutaria as Rebecca: Poised and self-assured.
›Huma Qureshi as Elizabeth: Menacing presence.
›Rukmini Vasanth as Melissa: Full-throttle action.

For months, the marketing of Toxic: A Fairy Tale for Grown-Ups has been an exercise in controlled withholding. Teasers arrived showing Yash clean-shaven and dangerous, bathed in neon light, radiating the kind of quiet menace he perfected as Rocky Bhai. Director Geetu Mohandas let the atmosphere do the talking — dark, stylish, a little unhinged. But the question everyone had been asking since the project was announced never got answered: who are the women?

https://youtube.com/watch?v=wya96yCsZZY

Now we know. And the roster is absurd.

The newly released "Ladies & Ladies" teaser introduces the five female leads of Toxic in a montage that trades exposition for mood, character bios for vibes. Nayanthara plays Ganga — appearing with the kind of still, commanding authority that suggests she's running whatever room she walks into. Kiara Advani, marking her Kannada debut, plays Nadia, and her brief glimpse balances vulnerability with quiet intensity that's miles from the rom-com energy she's built her career on. Tara Sutaria is Rebecca, poised and self-assured. Huma Qureshi brings menace as Elizabeth. And Rukmini Vasanth rounds out the ensemble as Melissa, appearing in what looks like a full-throttle action sequence.

!Fairy Tale — Photo: Wikimedia Commons

*"The teaser opens with a playfully unhinged disclaimer: "Kids… stay away."**

Five women. Five distinct presences. Not one of them reduced to a love interest.

The teaser opens with a playfully unhinged disclaimer: "Kids… stay away. Parents… make sure your kids stay away. Grandparents… make sure your kids' kids stay away. Great grandparents… at your own risk." What follows is drenched in the same neon-pink palette that's become the film's visual signature — nightclub lighting, leather, danger, and a haunting female voiceover that cuts through it all:

"Love makes monsters of women. It is a beautiful illusion, if one understands the depth of its deception."

Then Yash arrives, clean-shaven and lethal, squaring off against a group of women in what appears to be a bar fight choreographed by someone who studied both John Wick and Sanjay Leela Bhansali. He delivers the teaser's final line with the kind of smirk that's either incredibly charming or incredibly reckless: "Ladies and ladies. Do you want to come one at a time or all together?"

Reader, the internet had opinions.

The teaser has polarised audiences in a way that feels genuinely interesting rather than simply messy. The fan camp is electrified — this is Yash's return to the screen after a four-year absence since KGF: Chapter 2, and they're treating every frame like a sacred relic. Film critic Taran Adarsh and entertainment accounts have amplified the buzz, noting the film's potential to be a major pan-Indian event. The sceptics, meanwhile, are calling the aesthetic overdone and the swagger borrowed. The truth, as always in Indian cinema, will be settled at the box office on August 26.

!Rocky Bhai — Photo: Wikimedia Commons

Toxic's Multi-Lingual Strategy
›Shot in Kannada and English.
›Dubbed versions in Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam.
›Aims for a pan-India audience.
›Wide availability in overseas markets.
›Connects NRI audiences with diverse cast.

What's not in dispute is the ambition. Toxic has been shot simultaneously in Kannada and English, with dubbed versions dropping in Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, and Malayalam — making it a genuine pan-India play. Yash reportedly plays a massive dual role, and Mohandas — whose previous work includes the critically acclaimed Moothon — is bringing an arthouse director's eye to a mass-market gangster saga. Period setting. Underworld intrigue. Five women whose characters are defined by danger and desire rather than domesticity.

For Kiara Advani, this is a particularly significant departure. She's been the reigning queen of Bollywood rom-coms and family entertainers — Satyaprem Ki Katha, Bhool Bhulaiyaa 2 — and now here she is, taking a sudden pivot to a Kannada-English gangster film where she's named Nadia and exists in a world where love makes monsters. That's range, and it's exactly the kind of career move that either redefines an actress or confuses an audience. Either way, it's compelling to watch.

For Nayanthara, it's a chance to do what she does best — command the frame without needing to explain herself. For Tara Sutaria, it's the meatiest brief she's had in years. For Huma Qureshi, who's spent recent years toggling between OTT thrillers and Bollywood comedies, "Elizabeth" looks like a return to the kind of intensity she first showed in Gangs of Wasseypur. And Rukmini Vasanth — the Kannada industry's rising star — gets to stake her claim on a national stage for the first time.

The supporting cast includes Akshay Oberoi, Sudev Nair, and Amit Tiwari. The film is produced by KVN Productions in association with Monster Mind Creations.

Audience Reactions to the Teaser
›Electrified fan camp after Yash's return.
›Critics note potential for a major pan-Indian event.
›Skeptics call the aesthetic overdone.
›Social media buzz indicates high anticipation.
›Release date: August 26.

For NRI audiences, the pan-India release strategy means Toxic will be widely available in overseas markets across multiple languages — Hindi screenings in the US, UK, and Canada are virtually guaranteed given the star power involved. This broad accessibility is a major draw for the diaspora, allowing families to connect over shared cinematic experiences regardless of their location. Many NRIs eagerly anticipate films that bridge regional Indian cinema with a global appeal, and Toxic's multi-lingual release caters directly to this demand, making it a significant event for those looking to stay connected to Indian entertainment. The buzz on social media among the diaspora suggests a high level of anticipation, with many expressing excitement about seeing such a diverse cast in a high-octane production. Mark August 26 on your calendar.

The fairy tale has begun. Just make sure the children aren't watching.
author: Diaspora Desk
